scope: Fresh frozen synthetic transcript holdout, version 2. All podcast/host identities, sponsor contexts, timings, and reference intervals are authored. Word-aligned cases use authored token times, not observed speech. This is an evaluation-only challenge and does not measure real-podcast or unseen-speaker accuracy. Ambiguous cases require review without a definitive ad label.

cases.description: One paid sponsor block with product information and a closing acknowledgement; the following interview resumes the episode.

segments.text: The lock keeper remembers when all of these gates were moved by hand.
This part of the show is brought to you by Slate Finch work gloves.
The reinforced palm helps protect your hands during everyday garden jobs.
Use code GATE for ten percent off. Thanks to Slate Finch for sponsoring this episode.
Back to our conversation with the lock keeper: how many people worked each gate?

cases.description: The host jokes about a real paid sponsor product and makes an actual offer. The humorous sentences belong to the paid read.

segments.text: The next stop on our route is an abandoned customs house.
This is our paid message from Willow Wire cable organizers.
I tried their pouch and my charging leads have finally stopped auditioning for a knot museum.
Use code TANGLE for fifteen percent off a pouch. Sadly it cannot organize my thoughts.
Thanks to Willow Wire for supporting the episode.
Now back to the customs house and the records found in its cellar.

cases.description: The performer identifies a self-written, unpaid fake sponsor sketch. The offer and sponsor name are characters in the comedy.

segments.text: I wrote a fake sponsor sketch for the open mic. This is unpaid comedy, not a real business.
This episode is sponsored by Spare Tuesday, the company that sells an extra weekday.
Use code CALENDAR and your first Tuesday is free.
Our imaginary staff are available every eighth day. That is the end of the sketch.
How did the audience react when you performed it?

cases.description: An interview examines a recorded sales pitch as evidence; quoted ad language is not a live sponsor message.

segments.text: You brought the audio from the campaign that your paper investigated.
Yes. The announcer says, quote, this show is sponsored by Copper Meadow meals.
Then comes, use code DINNER for a free trial of the meal plan, end quote.
That wording mattered because the trial enrolled people in a recurring charge.
We are examining the campaign, not offering or endorsing the service.

cases.description: Independent repair history includes a product name, but no sales pitch or financial arrangement.

segments.text: This is a Birch Vale sewing machine from the late nineteen sixties.
The motor came from a different factory than the one used in the earlier model.
Birch Vale changed the mounting bracket to make repairs easier.
The museum bought this machine at an estate sale; the maker has no connection with our show.
Listen for the click when the mechanism engages.

cases.description: The host interrupts editorial content to sell a paid workshop; the introduction of that paid offer is included.

segments.text: There is one last repair technique to discuss after this announcement.
My paid bookbinding workshop is taking reservations for next month.
You get two classes, materials, and feedback on the notebook you make.
Use code BIND to save twenty dollars before registration closes.
Now back to the repair. The old adhesive has to soften before we lift the cloth.

cases.description: The purchase offer has finished before two ordinary interview sentences; a later return phrase does not make those sentences commercial.

segments.text: The weather instruments here were installed before the building opened.
This episode is sponsored by Ember Rail socks.
Use code STATION for twenty percent off your first order of Ember Rail socks.
The pressure gauge was calibrated every Monday by the same technician.
She kept the readings in a notebook that is now held in the local archive.
Now back to the instruments and their place in the station.

cases.description: A single unaligned segment contains editorial at 0-6, a paid read at 6-18, then editorial at 18-24 seconds. No word timestamps support an exact internal cut.

segments.text: The kiln needs several hours to cool. This episode is sponsored by Mallow Mug. Use code FIRING for ten dollars off the ceramic travel cup. Now back to the kiln and the way the glaze changes color.

cases.description: One transcript segment spans editorial speech and a complete paid read. Authored word timestamps make sentence-level commercial boundaries available.

segments.text: The bridge opens twice every morning. This episode is sponsored by Hazel Lamp. Use code BRIDGE for a free trial of its rechargeable reading light. Now back to the bridge keeper. The machinery underneath dates from the original construction.

cases.description: Two separate paid messages are divided by editorial discussion. The intervening episode content must remain.

segments.text: Today we are listening to the machines in an old textile mill.
This episode is sponsored by Rose Harbor earplugs.
Use code MILL for ten percent off your order. Thanks to Rose Harbor for sponsoring us.
Now back to the mill. The loom runs at a steady rhythm.
The operator learned to spot a broken thread by listening to that rhythm.
This next paid message is from Linden Case. Its carrying cases protect small recording equipment.
Use code SOUND for a free trial. Thanks to Linden Case for supporting the show.
Now back to the loom operator.
She is about to restart the machine after replacing a belt.

cases.description: A favorable account of a supplied product lacks evidence establishing whether mentioning it was a commercial obligation. No definitive ad label is supplied.

segments.text: The people at Ridge Parcel sent over one of their bags last week.
I used it on the train and the straps felt comfortable.
We had been talking about doing something together on the show.
I will have to check the messages before I explain the arrangement.
For now I can show you how the recorder fits in the front pocket.

cases.description: A short opening sponsor message ends before the actual show introduction. All offer language is commercial.

segments.text: This podcast is sponsored by Bright Loom notebooks.
The stitched binding lies flat and the pages are thick enough for ink drawings.
Order today with code LOOM for fifteen percent off. Thank you to Bright Loom for sponsoring us.
Welcome back. Our guest restores signs painted on the sides of old shops.
We met her on a narrow street behind the market.

cases.description: A sincere sponsorship read includes sarcasm about the host, not a claim that the sponsor is fictional.

segments.text: I spent yesterday measuring the rooms in the old observatory.
Our sponsor Quill Kettle paid for this message, so here is the official boiling announcement.
Its compact kettle heats one cup at a time, ideal for my ambitious schedule of making exactly one cup.
The actual offer is ten dollars off when you use code STEAM.
Thanks to Quill Kettle for sponsoring this episode.
Now back to the observatory measurements.

cases.description: A host introduces an unpaid fictional commercial as part of a radio comedy performance; its sales claims are editorial entertainment.

segments.text: We staged an unpaid radio comedy scene, including this entirely fictional commercial.
This portion is brought to you by Invisible Umbrella, guaranteed not to obstruct your view.
Order today and use code NOTHING for a free trial of absolutely nothing.
The joke is that there is no umbrella and no company. Nobody is selling anything here.
The actors then return to the scene at the bus stop.

cases.description: A listener quotes the terms of an old promotion during a consumer interview. The segment is an account of a disputed transaction.

segments.text: What exactly did the recording promise when you signed up?
It said, use code PANTRY for a free trial of the Cinder Basket food box.
I am repeating the offer I heard, not recommending it to anyone.
The charge that followed was the reason I contacted your consumer program.
The company did not fund this interview.

cases.description: A consumer-protection passage contains cue words about a free trial but advises against an unwanted subscription.

segments.text: A listener asked how to leave the Alder Ledger subscription.
If you cancel your free trial, save the confirmation number and check the next statement.
This is practical consumer advice; Alder Ledger has no involvement in this episode.
An unwanted renewal is easier to dispute when you keep the original terms.
Our next caller has a question about a different service.

cases.description: A paid membership pitch is distinct from an ordinary request to follow a free show.

segments.text: I have opened a paid membership for listeners who want the extra drawing lessons.
It costs six dollars a month and includes a live session with me every other week.
Use code SKETCH for your first month free before the regular monthly price begins.
Now back to the lesson. We start with the outline of the roof.
The shadows are longest on the northern side of this building.

cases.description: A finished sponsor message is followed by an editorial exchange before the explicit return marker. Preserve the exchange.

segments.text: The guest has brought a sample from the old sound archive.
This episode is sponsored by Wren Shelf headphones.
Use code ARCHIVE to save twenty dollars on a Wren Shelf pair.
That hiss comes from the original recording medium, not the playback equipment.
Now back to the archive and the work needed to preserve it.

cases.description: Authored internal times are editorial 0-5, self-promotion 5-15, editorial 15-23 seconds. The segment has no word alignment, so a confident whole-segment cut is unsupported.

segments.text: The lettering was carved by hand. My paid sign-painting class is now open; use code BRUSH to save thirty dollars on enrollment. Now back to the lettering and the tools used to shape it.

cases.description: The paid offer shares one display segment with editorial lead-in and return speech, with authored word boundaries for all tokens.

segments.text: The old receiver still picks up distant stations. This podcast is sponsored by Rowan Cord. Use code RADIO to save fifteen dollars on a replacement audio cable. Thanks to Rowan Cord for sponsoring this episode. Now back to the receiver and its unusual tuning mechanism.

cases.description: One external sponsor and one host-owned paid offer interrupt different parts of the conversation. Each needs its own interval.

segments.text: The guest is describing how she records the sound of rain.
This episode is sponsored by Heath Cover microphone shields.
Use code RAIN for fifteen percent off a shield. Thanks to Heath Cover for sponsoring us.
Now back to the recording. A sheltered doorway can change the sound dramatically.
The microphone position matters more than the size of the room.
My paid location-recording workshop is now available for enrollment.
Use code FIELD to save twenty dollars on the workshop before Sunday.
Now back to our guest and the recordings she made near the river.
The water sounded different after the rainfall ended.

cases.description: An enthusiastic recommendation mentions a business relationship without disclosing its commercial terms or whether this mention was agreed. Review is appropriate.

segments.text: I have been trying the Tern Table planner, and it has helped me keep track of the trip.
The company and I have been working on something this season.
I cannot explain the details of that arrangement in this excerpt.
The weekly pages are the part I have used most so far.
I will tell you more when we return from the trip.

cases.description: A midroll includes a sponsor acknowledgement after a clear purchase offer. The acknowledgement remains part of the ad.

segments.text: The railway signal changed the way trains passed through this junction.
A quick word from our sponsor, Elm Crest travel towels.
Their compact towel dries quickly and folds into a small pouch.
Use code JOURNEY for ten percent off. Thanks to Elm Crest for making this paid message possible.
Now back to the junction. The signal operator worked in the tower beside the tracks.

cases.description: The host calls their performance silly while explicitly confirming that the sponsorship and offer are real.

segments.text: The next interview starts with a walk through the market.
Maple Latch paid for this sponsorship, and they have allowed me one very silly voice.
Behold their lunch box, keeper of sandwiches and sworn enemy of loose crumbs.
The performance is silly but the offer is real: use code LUNCH for a free trial.
Thanks to Maple Latch for sponsoring us.
Now back to the market and its early morning deliveries.

cases.description: The speaker explicitly refuses sponsorship and performs an unpaid joke about an imaginary service; sponsor language is part of the joke.

segments.text: This sketch has no sponsor and nobody paid for it. I invented the following business for a joke.
This episode is sponsored by Remote Fog, bringing artisanal mist to your hallway.
Use code MIST for a free trial, although your hallway may never forgive you.
There is no Remote Fog shop; this was an unpaid comedy bit about lifestyle advertising.
Our guest laughs and tells us about an actual foggy morning at the harbor.

cases.description: An academic plays sponsor copy to study its rhetoric. Explicit quotations and their stated research purpose make this editorial content.

segments.text: We are analyzing how a sponsor read builds a sense of friendship with the listener.
The sample begins, quote, this episode is sponsored by Juniper Ferry travel packs.
The presenter then says, use code FRIEND for twenty percent off, end quote.
The words are part of our research material, and the company has not supported this program.
Our next point concerns the personal anecdote placed before that offer.

cases.description: An independent historical account discusses a branded object and a purchase made years earlier, without a current commercial offer.

segments.text: The archivist bought this Stone Finch typewriter at a street sale in nineteen ninety.
Stone Finch made a narrower carriage for the export version.
The unusual spacing in the letters comes from a damaged part in this particular machine.
We are describing an object in the archive, and have no connection with its manufacturer.
The next letter was typed on a different machine.

cases.description: The host promotes a paid digital collection with specific benefits and a current offer. It is commercial self-promotion.

segments.text: The discussion of the photographs will continue after this announcement.
I am selling a new digital collection of my coastal photography lessons.
It includes eight recorded classes and the worksheets I use in each one.
Use code COAST to save twenty dollars when you buy the collection this week.
Now back to the photographs. The light changed just before the boat entered the harbor.

cases.description: A clear ad finishes before unrelated historical content, even though a conversational return phrase appears later.

segments.text: The museum has preserved the original workshop benches.
This episode is sponsored by Alder Mill aprons.
Use code BENCH for a free trial of the Alder Mill workshop apron.
The smaller bench was used by apprentices, who began with simple repairs.
The master craftsperson checked every joint before the furniture left the room.
Now back to our tour of the workshop.

cases.description: One unaligned segment mixes editorial at 0-7, humorous paid promotion at 7-19, and editorial at 19-26 seconds. The missing word times require review despite clear commercial intent.

segments.text: The clock has been running for over a century. This paid message is from Bracken Bell alarms; mine gets me out of bed with all the diplomacy of a brass band. Use code WAKE for ten percent off. Now back to the clock and its carefully maintained gears.

cases.description: Word timestamps make it possible to separate a humorous paid message from editorial sentences within the same display segment.

segments.text: The baker opens the shop before sunrise. This is a paid advertisement for Clover Tin lunch boxes. My sandwich has finally acquired a respectable address. Use code BREAD for a free trial of the box. Thanks to Clover Tin for sponsoring the show. Now back to the baker and the first batch of loaves.

cases.description: Two actual sponsor blocks surround an explicitly unpaid comic aside. The comic sponsor imitation in the middle is not part of either commercial interval.

segments.text: This episode is sponsored by Winter Thread jackets.
Use code COLD for ten percent off. Thanks to Winter Thread for supporting the show.
Now back to our guest, who has written an unpaid fake sponsor joke for the comedy section.
Our imaginary sponsor is Emergency Sunshine, which rents a tiny sun for your coat pocket.
There is no business or offer behind that joke. Let us return to the interview.
A paid message now from Hollow Oak flasks, the second real sponsor of this episode.
Use code WARM for a free trial of the insulated flask. Thanks to Hollow Oak for sponsoring us.
Now back to the guest and the story of her winter journey.

cases.description: The host received a product and discussed mentioning it, but the excerpt establishes neither paid placement nor an independent editorial purpose. No definitive class is asserted.

segments.text: Fallow Press gave me a copy of the new field journal before it went on sale.
I told them I might discuss it when we recorded the next episode.
There were other messages about the collaboration that are not covered here.
The paper held up better than I expected in the rain.
I have brought it along so we can look at the pages together.
